items.title: How a two-way door calcifies into a one-way door
items.description: Models this unit's own lock-in point: the DSL's reversal cost isn't fixed at the moment the decision is made — it climbs as more things (config strings written by other services) come to depend on it. "Base rewrite cost" is what reversing the decision would cost with zero dependents (still real — deleting an interpreter and its call sites is work — but small). Each dependent adds its own migration cost, since every stored config string written in the DSL's syntax has to be rewritten by hand if the DSL goes away. Defaults (2 dependents so far, 3 days per dependent) reproduce an early-but-already-slipping state: reversal already costs more than the DSL saved on day one. Drag dependents up to 8+ (Northlane eight months from now) to see reversal cost cross well past what building the legible version would have cost from the start — the same threshold L3's ADR was written to avoid crossing.

params.name: numberOfDependents
params.label: Services/configs now depending on the DSL's syntax

params.name: baseRewriteCost
params.label: Base cost to remove the interpreter itself

items.compute: const dependents = params.numberOfDependents; const perDependent = params.migrationCostPerDependent; const base = params.baseRewriteCost; const reversalCost = base + dependents * perDependent; const legibleFromStartCost = 6; return { reversalCost: Math.round(reversalCost * 10) / 10, legibleFromStartCost };

outputs.label: Cost to reverse the DSL decision now
What building the legible version would have cost from day one
